analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA temporarily import foreign versions of prescription drugs during shortages and in markets with little competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a prescription drug is in shortage, or when an old drug (approved 10+ years, patents expired) is sold by fewer than five companies, the FDA would have to let importers bring in versions of that drug approved in trusted foreign countries. Importation would start within 60 days of a qualifying application and last up to three years or until the shortage ends. The FDA could still refuse any import it judged unsafe or ineffective. The goal is to end shortages of old, cheap, lifesaving drugs and break up markets where a handful of manufacturers face no competition.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who rely on old, inexpensive, lifesaving drugs — the kind that repeatedly go into shortage when only a few manufacturers make them. The bill would force the FDA to open a temporary import pathway (starting within 60 days of a qualifying application, lasting up to three years) for foreign-approved versions of shortage drugs, and would treat markets with fewer than five approved versions of a 10-plus-year-old, patent-expired drug as de facto shortages, triggering importation and faster FDA review. Hospitals, pharmacists, and generic-competition advocates would also benefit from a more reliable supply.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients facing shortages of old, cheap drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FDA to temporarily authorize importation of a prescription drug that is lifesaving, life-sustaining, or treats a debilitating condition when the drug is in shortage, is approved abroad, and has the same active ingredient as the drug in short supply.
Importation must begin within 60 days of a qualifying application and lasts up to three years or until the shortage ends.

Treats drugs in 'marginally competitive markets' — fewer than five approved versions commercially available, approved at least 10 years, with expired active-ingredient patents — as being in shortage, triggering importation and expedited FDA reviews and inspections.
Requires annual reporting on the number of drugs authorized for temporary importation, so Congress and the public can track use of the authority.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers whose products sit in shortage-prone, low-competition markets — they would face temporary foreign competition for up to three years and lose some of the pricing power that comes from being one of only a few approved suppliers. The FDA would also bear new work: processing importation applications, deciding on denials, and expediting reviews and inspections, plus an annual report on drugs imported under the authority.

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the FDA discretion to deny any importation it judges unsafe or ineffective, but speeding foreign-sourced drugs into the supply chain still carries some safety risk, which is the objection drug manufacturers and safety-focused reviewers would raise.

The bill treats a 'marginally competitive market' as a shortage even when supply is adequate, which addresses persistent high prices and thin supply but does not fix the underlying economics that push manufacturers out of low-margin old drugs in the first place.
The bill received no committee hearing, markup, or vote, so its design was never tested or refined through the normal legislative process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: fewer dangerous shortages of old, cheap, lifesaving drugs, and more competition in markets where a handful of manufacturers have the field to themselves. The costs are modest and mostly fall on the pharmaceutical industry, though an honest supporter would acknowledge that forcing faster foreign importation carries some safety risk even with the FDA's discretion to deny unsafe drugs, and that the bill does nothing to fix the underlying reasons manufacturers leave these low-margin markets in the first place. The bill died without any committee action, so its costs were never debated on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Health Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: S. 917 was introduced on March 23, 2021 by Sen. Klobuchar with Sens. Lee, Durbin, and Grassley.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
It attracted only three cosponsors — two Senate Republicans and one Senate Democrat — over its two-year lifespan.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The brand-name and generic drug makers whose old drugs would have faced forced foreign competition keep their thin-market pricing power, and the Senate Health Committee's inaction means the shortage and price problems the bill targeted went unaddressed by Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers with little competition, and the status quo

for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Senate Committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor joined by Republicans Lee and Grassley and Democrat Durbin — but total support stayed thin at four senators, and no party bloc ever had to vote on it because the committee never acted.

industries.industry: Brand-name and generic drug makers in low-competition markets
industries.note: The bill forces temporary foreign competition into markets where fewer than five versions of an old drug are sold, and lets importers bring in competing supply during shortages. This erodes the pricing power that comes from being one of a few approved suppliers, and patients get steadier access and lower prices as a result.

The bill opens a new, temporary pathway for foreign-approved versions of shortage drugs to enter the U.S. market, a business opportunity for manufacturers and importers abroad. Their gain runs alongside the public's interest in ending shortages, though it depends on FDA safety review.
